A commenter said they have always loved Gumroad's simplicity for both creators and buyers.

Several users complained that Gumroad's released code is not open source. They said its license fails the OSD, is 'very limiting for Business,' and that it should be called 'source available.' One asked for MIT or AGPL instead.

One user liked that Gumroad's code license allows use up to $1M in revenue before you must rebuild. They called it a 'game changer' for building an MVP of a Gumroad-like app and said they prefer it to GPL, though MIT would be ideal.

A user grepped Gumroad's codebase to see which vendors you'd need relationships with to run it. They found PayPal and Stripe for payments, TaxJar, Vatstack and IRAS for tax, SendGrid, EasyPost, OpenAI, Iffy and Helper.ai for AI moderation and support, Dropbox, and others.
Users complained that Gumroad's repo README jumps straight into installation and gives almost no information about what the product actually does.

A user received two spam emails from legitimate Gumroad addresses. In each, a seller had 'sold' them a $0 item whose description contained a cryptocurrency scam. Gumroad's abuse form is a Google Form that only allows one response, so they couldn't report both, and they weren't sure abuse@gumroad.com was monitored.
Early Show HN feedback: the proposed 30% cut was widely called too high. One commenter said 5–10% would be acceptable, and another said the simplicity justifies a higher cut, but maybe not 30%.
Early users pointed out that once a buyer paid and reached the destination link, they could trivially share that link. They suggested hosting the files on Gumroad's servers or checking the referrer.
Early reactions praised it as 'the simplest way to sell digital goods' and as a great idea with good execution. They saw speed and ease of use as the big selling point.
A tester got a broken lock icon and a 'Connection partially encrypted' warning, caused by Google Fonts being loaded over http. Another user hit a BadKeyError traceback in the sessions code.

Feature requests from the launch thread: a pay-what-you-want option with a minimum price, a limit on the number of downloads, a preview of the content before paying, and Markdown in product descriptions so links are clickable.
A summary of the linked article said Gumroad replaced customer support with poor AI chatbots that offer no escalation to humans.

An affiliate earned a $17 sale, but payout required escalating identity verification: name, address, the last 4 digits of their SSN, then the full SSN plus an ID upload. Each step 'failed to verify' with no reason given. Support ignored them for over 2 weeks. They emailed the CEO, who paid them personally via Zelle within hours.

A user who had planned to sell a PDF book through Gumroad said they now want alternatives because of the CEO's DOGE work. Another urged creators to switch to Patreon, Stripe, BuyMeACoffee or Ko-fi and asked for a migration guide.
A user said Gumroad began rolling out Merchant of Record tax charges before the feature was finished. They said it was being applied globally, including in regions with no tax system to collect for.
A commenter called Gumroad 'an amazing idea' because any platform that helps people just try pushing out products is a win.
